say.text: Ravi, 34, otherwise healthy. Twenty hours of right upper quadrant pain, WBC 14,000/mm³, no organ failure and no tender mass on examination.
Which **TG18 grade** is he?

choices.label: Grade II, WBC of 14,000 is clearly high
Grade I, mild, no organ failure
Grade II, pain has lasted over 24 hours
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. He has no Grade II marker: 14,000 is under the 18,000 line and his pain is far under 72 hours. With no organ failure he is Grade I.

choices.label: I know the grades, skip the criteria

say.text: Grade II needs any one of: WBC above 18,000/mm³, a tender palpable RUQ mass, complaints over 72 hours, or marked local inflammation.
Grade III needs organ dysfunction in any one system. Grade I is neither, in an otherwise healthy patient.
Not the right choice.
A WBC of 14,000 is above the routine lab flag of 10,000, which is why it tempts you. TG18 sets its own, higher count for Grade II.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the Grade II list again before you commit to a grade.

say.text: Not the right choice.
Twenty hours of pain feels prolonged, so a 24-hour line tempts you. TG18 sets a far longer duration bar for Grade II.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the Grade II duration bar before you commit to a grade.

say.text: Test Ravi against each Grade II marker in turn: the WBC, a tender mass, the days of pain, and local inflammation.
Set Ravi beside a Grade II patient with a WBC of 19,000 and a tender RUQ mass. Ravi has neither marker, and his pain has run only 20 hours.
He meets no Grade II criterion and no organ failure, so the grade with neither is the answer.
Which single finding is enough, on its own, for TG18 **Grade II** acute cholecystitis?
Yes. Any one Grade II marker is enough, and the WBC line sits well above a routine lab flag, at more than 18,000/mm³.
Not the right choice.
10,000/mm³ is the routine leukocytosis flag on a lab sheet, so it feels like the Grade II line. TG18 sets that line higher.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the Grade II WBC line is worth a second look before you commit.

say.text: Not the right choice.
Complaints over 24 hours sound long for a gallbladder attack, so they tempt you. The TG18 duration bar for Grade II is much longer.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the Grade II duration bar is worth a second look before you commit.

say.text: Not the right choice.
A count of 12,000 with fever is the pattern of a routine infection on a lab report. Grade II uses its own, higher count, with no fever condition.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the Grade II WBC line is worth a second look before you commit.

say.text: Grade II is a set of separate markers, each a clear abnormality rather than a routine lab flag. The WBC line is above 18,000/mm³ and the duration line is above 72 hours.
Which single value meets a **Grade III** organ criterion on its own?
Yes. Renal dysfunction counts when creatinine is above 2.0 mg/dL or there is oliguria, and one system is enough for Grade III.
Not the right choice.
1.5 mg/dL is the familiar ceiling on a routine renal panel, so it looks like the severe line. The Grade III renal bar is set higher.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the Grade III renal bar before you commit.

say.text: Not the right choice.
An INR of 1.2 looks like a bleeding warning on a coagulation report. The Grade III hepatic bar is a higher INR than that.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the Grade III hepatic bar before you commit.

say.text: Not the right choice.
150,000 is the lower limit on a routine platelet count, so a value under it tempts you. The Grade III haematological bar is lower.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the Grade III platelet bar before you commit.

say.text: Grade III needs organ dysfunction in one system: noradrenaline for hypotension, reduced consciousness, PaO2/FiO2 below 300, creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL or oliguria, PT-INR above 1.5, or platelets below 100,000/mm³.
A fit adult has acute calculous cholecystitis. What is the **current treatment of choice** for the index admission?

choices.label: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in this admission
Conservative treatment, then interval surgery at 6-8 weeks
Antibiotics alone, operate only if symptoms recur
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission, ideally within 72 hours, is preferred. It shortens the stay without more complications.
Not the right choice.
This is the older plan that many PYQ keys still carry, so it feels like the standard answer. Current practice differs, so check the key before you commit.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the teach-both point: the PYQ key and current practice are not the same.

say.text: Not the right choice.
Antibiotics settle the first attack, so waiting for a recurrence feels safe. The guidance favours surgery in the same admission.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check when the guidance puts surgery before you commit.

say.text: Not the right choice.
Drainage is a real treatment, so it tempts you as a safe first move. It is reserved for patients too ill or high-risk for surgery.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check who drainage is for before you commit.

say.text: Ask two questions: is this patient fit for an operation, and when does current practice put that operation?
Take two fit patients with the same stone. Both are operated in the admission they arrive in, and the 6-8 week wait is the older key, not the default.
An elderly man has acute cholecystitis, hypotension on noradrenaline and a raised creatinine. What is the **first management**?

choices.label: Conservative care, interval surgery at 6-8 weeks
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Noradrenaline and a raised creatinine mean Grade III, so organ support comes first and drainage is the usual first step. Surgery is for selected fit patients later.
Not the right choice.
Early laparoscopic surgery is the answer for a fit patient, so it tempts you for any gallbladder. This patient is on noradrenaline, so grade and fitness come first.

say.text: Ask two questions: how sick is this patient right now, and what does that mean for surgery in the first hours?
Hypotension needing noradrenaline is a Grade III organ marker. Grade III patients get organ support and usually drainage first, and early surgery is for selected fit patients at advanced centres.
Grade II acute cholecystitis in a patient unfit for surgery. Which plan is right, in order?

choices.label: Medical treatment or drainage first, surgery deferred
Cholecystectomy at once in the index admission
Cholecystectomy only after 6-8 weeks in every patient
Open cholecystectomy at once, to be safe

say.text: Yes. Grade II is treated by early surgery only when the patient is fit, so an unfit patient gets medical treatment or drainage and surgery is deferred.
Not the right choice.
